newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel hopes for Amsterdam deal on EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel hopes for Amsterdam deal on EMU pact.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday he hoped European leaders could still reach agreement next week on a fiscal stability pact to ensure discipline after the euro launch.

Waigel told a meeting of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), that Germany and France were not at odds over the need for the stability pact after Friday's Franco-German summit.
"I hope we can still reach an agreement," said Waigel, who will meet EU finance ministers on Sunday night in Amsterdam ahead of Monday's EU summit where the pact will be a top issue.
Later, at a CSU meeting in Schwabmuenchen, Waigel said an end was also in sight in the government's dispute with the Bundesbank over plans to revalue gold and currency reserves.
Waigel said weekend talks among European officials would centre on France's demand for greater emphasis on job creation, an issue he said Germany was not completely against.

France's new Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin said on Friday after the summit that Paris was committed to a single currency but that growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the stability pact limiting budget deficits.

"The issue of the stability pact has not been put into question by the new French government," Waigel said. "Not a single comma, not a single period and not a single word will be changed. Everyone must know that."
"The question is whether we can reach agreement over the issue of employment and whether we can say more," Waigel said.

France is expected to receive concessions on job issues through two political declarations that will accompany the EMU stability pact. The declarations will call for stronger links between job creation and the new euro, set to start in 1999.

Waigel, architect of the stability pact approved last year in Dublin and due for approval at the Amsterdam summit, said Bonn was committed to fighting unemployment levels that reached post-war records earlier in the year.
But he said Germany remained committed to the need for the stability pact to ensure credibility for the new currency, a requirement to win the support of the German public.
"We must take them seriously," Waigel said of opinion polls showing opposition among a majority of the the German public to exchanging the mark for a weaker currency.

"The mark is more than just a currency," he said. "It is part of the identity of Germany, one struck even before we won our first Olympic gold medal or first world soccer championship. There is only one answer to win support - stability, stability and once more stability."

Waigel reaffirmed his insistence that nations seeking to join currency union at the start in January 1999 must have a deficit level of 3.0 percent or less of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), a level many economists say Germany itself cannot reach.
Many leading German officials have said Waigel must back off his insistence on the 3.0 percent level in order to save currency union from being delayed or abandoned all together.
But some top CSU officials have said fulfilling the entry criteria laid out in the Maastricht Treaty are more important than following the timeline to start EMU on schedule.

"Discussions over whether the criteria should be 3.2 percent or 3.3 percent are not necessary. If we allow that, then other countries will say 3.7 percent or 4.1 percent is OK and then we reach a point where the German public will no longer believe in the new currency," Waigel said.
Waigel also said a deal was in the offing with the Bundesbank over Bonn's controversial plans to revalue gold and currency reserves stored at the German central bank.

Unprecedented Bundesbank protests have forced Waigel to abort an original plan to use profits generated by asset revaluation to ease Germany's path into monetary union this year, the crucial year for choosing EMU entrants.

The precise terms of the new agreement are not clear but CSU sources at the afternoon meeting in Schwabmuenchen said talks on revaluing gold were still continuing, while it had been agreed to revalue currency reserves this year, but to effect a profit transfer only in 1998.
Waigel said the German economic climate has improved in recent months and predicted 1997 economic growth of about 2.5 percent and growth of 2.75 percent for next year.
"The economic climate has brightened," he said, noting lower interest rates, stable currency market rates and higher incoming orders among many German companies.
